title: Training the Whole Agent, Not Just the Model

paper.title: Training the Whole Agent, Not Just the Model
paper.abstract: Abstract Training coding agents typically updates the policy while keeping the harness fixed. During training, trajectories reveal flawed repair strategies and interaction problems that vary across tasks and change as the policy learns. We introduce HarnessAdapt-RL, which trains the policy and adapts its harness during reinforcement learning. For flawed repair strategies, a frozen teacher generates task-specific mechanism-level skills. For interaction problems recurring across tasks, a separate teacher model evolves tools and hooks, keeping each change only if it improves the observed pass rate or the observed trainable rate without lowering either. The policy trains with the adapted harness, and its new trajectories guide further adaptation. With a 9B base model, HarnessAdapt-RL improves pass@1 over GRPO by 9.8, 12.6, and 6.4 percentage points on SWE-bench Verified, Multilingual, and Pro, and outperforms GRPO with the human-designed OpenHands harness. Gains from mechanism-level skills persist after their removal at evaluation. Re-evolving tools and hooks as the policy changes outperforms freezing early versions. Removing them at deployment, in contrast, costs up to 7.7 percentage points. Training therefore produces a model–harness pair: the trained policy and the evolved tools and hooks, with skills removed at deployment.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: A coding agent operates as a model–harness pair: the model selects actions, while the harness provides guidance, tools, and runtime feedback. Agent training typically improves the policy while keeping the harness fixed [ Jain et al., 2025 , Yang et al., 2025a , Xi et al., 2026 ] . The harness shapes the interaction trajectories used to update the policy, affecting both the effectiveness of training and the performance of the trained agent [ Chen et al., 2026 ] . Prior work has explored both harness optimization and training-time guidance. Previous methods optimize the harness while keeping the policy fixed [ Lee et al., 2026a , Jiang et al., 2026 , Du et al., 2026 ] . Other methods use skills and training guidance to improve policy learning from trajectories [ Xiao et al., 2026 , Wang et al., 2026 , Shi et al., 2026 ] . Co-Harness alternates harness updates with supervised fine-tuning on trajectories generated by the improved harness [ Chen et al., 2026 ] . We study harness adaptation during reinforcement learning for coding agents. During training, trajectories expose flawed repair strategies, such as incorrect diagnoses or fixes that only address symptoms. They also reveal interaction problems, such as failed editing commands, excessive output, or insufficient verification. This evidence can guide changes to skills, tools, and runtime hooks that help alleviate these problems. As the problems vary across tasks and change with the policy, the harness needs to adapt throughout training (Appendix 9.3 ). We therefore ask how to design skills for policy learning, how to design and select tools and hooks as the policy changes, and which harness components to retain at deployment. To address these questions, we introduce HarnessAdapt-RL , which trains the policy and adapts its harness during reinforcement learning. In our setting, skills are textual guidance supplied to the policy during training. First, we compare three skill-guidance variants and use mechanism-level skills that explain when and why a repair strategy applies without providing concrete answers. A frozen teacher model generates these task-specific skills from training trajectories. Second, a separate teacher model identifies recurring interaction and feedback problems across tasks and proposes changes to tools and hooks. Harness selection considers both task success and the availability of rollouts for policy updates (Section 3.3 ). Each proposal is kept only if it improves the observed pass rate or the observed trainable rate without lowering either (Appendix 8.2 ). We refer to this process as tool and hook evolution. The policy then trains with GRPO [ Shao et al., 2024 ] on fresh rollouts using the evolved tools and hooks and skills for assisted tasks. Trajectories from the updated policy guide later proposals. Third, we examine which components should remain at deployment. We evaluate the policy after removing skills and compare performance with and without the evolved tools and hooks. With a 9B base model, HarnessAdapt-RL improves pass@1 over GRPO by 9.8, 12.6, and 6.4 percentage points on SWE-bench Verified [ Chowdhury et al., 2024 ] , Multilingual [ Yang et al., 2025a ] , and Pro [ Deng et al., 2025 ] . It also outperforms GRPO training with the human-designed OpenHands harness on all three benchmarks. Under the same base harness, models trained with mechanism-level skills perform best among the three skill-guidance variants when evaluated without skills. Re-evolving tools and hooks as the policy changes outperforms keeping their early versions fixed. Holding the trained policy weights fixed, removing the evolved tools and hooks at evaluation reduces pass@1 by up to 7.7 percentage points. Together, these results show that gains from skills persist after their removal, while the evolved tools and hooks remain necessary for full performance at deployment. Our contributions are threefold: • Skill design for policy learning. We compare three skill-guidance variants and find that mechanism-level skills yield the best repair performance after guidance is removed. • Tool and hook evolution during reinforcement learning. We use current-policy trajectories to propose tools and hooks and select changes using both the pass rate and the trainable rate. • Training and deploying the model–harness pair. We show that gains from skill guidance persist after its removal, while retaining the evolved tools and hooks at deployment preserves the complete performance.

sections.heading: 3 Method: Training the Whole Agent
sections.text: Figure 1 summarizes HarnessAdapt-RL. A teacher model uses current-policy trajectories to generate task-specific skills for flawed repair strategies. A separate teacher model proposes changes to tools and hooks for recurring interaction problems across tasks. We accept a proposal only if it improves the observed pass rate or the observed trainable rate without lowering either. The policy then trains through GRPO [ Shao et al., 2024 ] on rollouts generated with the adapted harness. Its new trajectories then guide subsequent harness adaptation.

sections.heading: 3.1 Policy-Adaptive Repair Skills
sections.text: We generate skills from training trajectories to guide the policy’s repair strategies. Prior work finds that many skills do not improve software engineering performance [ Han et al., 2026 ] . We therefore compare three ways of generating skills and assess the model’s performance after training, with the skills removed. We first evaluate a skill bank with a fixed capacity, based on prior work that extracts reusable strategies from trajectories [ Suzgun et al., 2025 , Xia et al., 2026 ] . The teacher reviews trajectories across training tasks and adds, removes, merges, or updates general repair skills. This approach does not consistently improve performance over GRPO, suggesting that these skills are too general to help with individual repair tasks (Section 4.3 ). A more task-specific alternative is to provide near-answer hints with concrete code changes, including variable, function, or class names. These hints produce shorter trajectories and higher training success, but the trained model performs worse than GRPO when evaluated without them (Section 4.3 , Appendix 9.2 ). We therefore propose mechanism-level skills that focus on the policy’s flawed repair strategies while leaving the policy to work out the concrete solution. For each assisted task, the teacher model compares two trajectories from the current policy. Using the issue and the evidence in these trajectories, it identifies a repair strategy and explains when and why it applies. The resulting mechanism-level skill retains the technical reasoning behind the repair but omits repository paths, code symbols, and literal code. This guides the policy’s repair strategy while leaving code localization and implementation to the policy. Appendices 7.2 and 10.2 provide generation details and examples.

sections.heading: 3.2 Evolving Tools and Hooks for Policy Training
sections.text: Training trajectories also reveal recurring problems in how the policy interacts with its environment. The teacher uses this evidence to propose changes to tools and hooks. To support both task performance and policy learning, it uses the pass rate and the trainable rate to guide these proposals. Trainable rollouts are those usable for policy updates (Appendix 8.2 ). The teacher uses current-policy trajectories and the current harness to develop a proposal in four steps. (1) Find recurring problems. The teacher compares trajectories across tasks to identify recurring problems in tool use and feedback. (2) Inspect trajectories. The teacher reads the tool calls, outputs, and hook messages to understand each recurring problem. For example, the policy runs fewer verification tests later in training, even though it has testing tools and receives reminders. The teacher inspects these trajectories to understand why the policy skips tests before submitting a patch. (3) Design changes. To address the identified problems, the teacher can propose one or more tools, hooks, or a combination of both. Tools package repair operations into reusable actions. Hooks give the policy feedback during execution. In the testing example, the teacher modifies the patch-preparation tool so that it automatically runs related tests when preparing a patch. A hook then reports any test failures and reminds the policy to check them before submission. (4) Implement the proposal. The teacher implements the proposed changes as a candidate harness for evaluation. As the policy learns, its new trajectories guide further adaptation of tools and hooks (Appendix 9.3 ). Appendix 8.2 provides the full proposal procedure.

sections.heading: 3.3 Training-Aware Harness Selection
sections.text: We select harness changes to support both task success and policy learning. GRPO uses reward differences among attempts on the same task to update the policy [ Shao et al., 2024 , Yu et al., 2025 ] . Groups in which all attempts succeed or all fail provide no reward contrast for policy updates. Successful rollouts in an all-success group therefore count toward the pass rate without contributing to policy learning. To account for training usability, we also measure the trainable rate, the fraction of sampled rollouts eligible for policy updates (Appendix 8.2 ). We evaluate each proposal by running the candidate and current harnesses with the same policy, tasks, skills, and rollout budget. We accept the proposal only if it improves the observed pass rate or the observed trainable rate without lowering either. These rates are empirical fractions from the finite comparison rollouts; the acceptance rule does not test statistical significance. Accepted changes are used for subsequent policy training. Otherwise, training continues with the current tools and hooks. Changes from a rejected proposal can be proposed again in later rounds.

sections.heading: Policy updates.
sections.text: After selection, we collect fresh rollouts with the selected tools and hooks, providing skills for assisted tasks. Preparation and comparison rollouts are not reused for training. We update the policy with GRPO using the new rollouts, with loss computed only on policy-generated tokens [ Shao et al., 2024 ] .

sections.heading: Evolution across training epochs.
sections.text: Each training epoch begins with up to five rounds of tool and hook evolution. After each round, we update the policy using the selected tools and hooks. These tools and hooks then stay fixed for the remaining training steps in that epoch. The first epoch produces H 1 H_{1} . The second epoch starts from H 1 H_{1} and uses trajectories from the updated policy to evolve H 2 H_{2} .

sections.heading: Training setup.
sections.text: We train on a fixed subset of the R2E-Gym-Lite training split [ Jain et al., 2025 ] , shared across all training configurations. The training tasks are disjoint from the evaluation benchmarks. In HarnessAdapt-RL, skills are provided for all training tasks in the first epoch and a fixed subset in the second. Appendix 7.1 details task selection and the assisted subset. Our base model is Qwen3.5-9B [ Qwen Team, 2026 ] , and the base harness H 0 H_{0} uses mini-swe-agent [ Yang et al., 2024 ] . We use the frozen GLM-5.3-Flash teacher [ Z.ai, 2026 ] to generate skills, and GPT-5.6 Sol [ OpenAI, 2026 ] through Codex [ OpenAI, 2025 ] to propose and implement tools and hooks. Appendix 8.1 records the model identifiers and access interfaces. Policy training uses GRPO [ Shao et al., 2024 ] . A submitted patch receives a reward of 1 if it passes the task tests and 0 otherwise. The GRPO baseline receives twice as many policy-training rollouts as the other trained configurations. Appendix 8 gives implementation details and hyperparameters, and Appendix 9.7 reports the additional costs of preparation, harness comparison, and teacher calls.

sections.heading: Configurations.
sections.text: Base model uses the initial policy and base harness H 0 H_{0} without training. GRPO trains the policy with H 0 H_{0} and no skills. OpenHands-GRPO uses the human-designed OpenHands harness, also without skills [ Wang et al., 2025 ] . To compare three ways of generating skills, Skill-Hint , Skill-Mechanism , and Skill-Bank use near-answer hints, mechanism-level skills, and general repair skills from a skill bank, respectively. All three train the policy with the base harness H 0 H_{0} . We compare three further configurations to test whether tools and hooks need to adapt as the policy learns. All three use mechanism-level skills during policy training. Our full method, HarnessAdapt-RL , alternates policy updates with tool and hook evolution in both epochs. Pre-Evolved tests whether evolving tools and hooks before policy training is enough. It follows the same search steps and uses the same tasks as HarnessAdapt-RL. However, the policy stays fixed at the base model throughout the search. It then trains the policy for two epochs with the resulting harness H pre H_{\mathrm{pre}} fixed. H 1 H_{1} +Mechanism tests whether tools and hooks need to evolve again in the second epoch. It shares the first epoch with HarnessAdapt-RL, so both start the second epoch with the same policy checkpoint and harness H 1 H_{1} . Both continue training the policy, but H 1 H_{1} +Mechanism keeps H 1 H_{1} fixed, while HarnessAdapt-RL evolves it into H 2 H_{2} . Appendix 9.6 reports additional fixed-harness configurations.

sections.heading: Evaluation.
sections.text: We report pass@1 on SWE-bench Verified [ Jimenez et al., 2024 , Chowdhury et al., 2024 ] , SWE-bench Multilingual [ Yang et al., 2025a ] , and SWE-bench Pro [ Deng et al., 2025 ] . Each evaluation run uses one attempt per task. We repeat each evaluation three times and report the mean pass@1. We assess statistical significance using paired bootstrap confidence intervals for performance differences (Appendix 9.4 ). All configurations use the same evaluation limits (Appendix 7.3 ). Evaluation uses no skills, teacher assistance, or further harness updates. Table 1 compares complete agents, each evaluated with its deployment harness.

sections.heading: HarnessAdapt-RL performs best on average.
sections.text: HarnessAdapt-RL achieves an average pass@1 of 44.9%, the highest in Table 1 , compared with 35.3% for GRPO. Its gains over GRPO are 9.8, 12.6, and 6.4 percentage points on Verified, Multilingual, and Pro, respectively. Both use the same 9B base model, and evaluation uses no skills or teacher calls.

sections.heading: The gains also hold against OpenHands-GRPO.
sections.text: OpenHands-GRPO trains the same base model with a human-designed harness instead of H 0 H_{0} . HarnessAdapt-RL exceeds it by 6.2, 4.0, and 7.4 percentage points on the three benchmarks. The advantage is therefore not limited to comparison with the minimal base harness.

sections.heading: Mechanism-level skills perform best after removal.
sections.text: The three skill variants use the same base harness H 0 H_{0} , so they compare different ways of generating skills. After the skills are removed, the model trained with mechanism-level skills reaches an average score of 38.3%, compared with 32.7% for near-answer hints and 34.1% for skill-bank generation. Only mechanism-level skills improve performance over GRPO on all three benchmarks. Near-answer hints achieve higher training success, but this does not lead to better performance without the hints (Section 4.3 ).

sections.heading: Evolution during training improves performance compared to pre-training search.
sections.text: Pre-Evolved uses the same search steps and tasks as HarnessAdapt-RL, but its policy remains at the base model throughout the search. Both configurations use mechanism-level skills when training the policy. HarnessAdapt-RL scores 2.4, 4.3, and 2.7 percentage points higher on Verified, Multilingual, and Pro. These results favor using trajectories from the updated policy to improve tools and hooks.

sections.heading: Evolving tools and hooks again in the second epoch improves performance.
sections.text: H 1 H_{1} +Mechanism and HarnessAdapt-RL share the first epoch and start the second with the same policy checkpoint and H 1 H_{1} . Both continue training the policy, but only HarnessAdapt-RL evolves the tools and hooks again. This raises pass@1 over H 1 H_{1} +Mechanism by 2.2, 4.6, and 2.0 percentage points on Verified, Multilingual, and Pro. Later trajectories show that the policy runs fewer verification tests despite having testing tools and reminders. The teacher changes the tool that prepares the patch so that it automatically runs related tests. A hook then reports any test failures and reminds the policy to check them before submission (Section 4.4 ).

sections.heading: 4.3 Why Mechanism-Level Skills?
sections.text: {wrapfloat} figureR0.48 Figure 2 : Training success and Verified performance without skills. Faint lines show individual updates, bold lines five-update trailing means; dashed lines separate the two training epochs. Figure 2 shows that skill-bank training closely follows GRPO in both training success and Verified performance. This suggests that its general repair strategies offer limited help for individual tasks. Near-answer hints increase training success substantially, but the trained model performs worse than GRPO after skills are removed. Mechanism-level skills improve training success while also achieving the best performance without skills. Higher success during training does not necessarily lead to better performance after training. To examine this difference, we first compare the rewards of attempts on the same task. GRPO uses these reward differences to update the policy [ Shao et al., 2024 , Yu et al., 2025 ] . When every attempt succeeds or every attempt fails, the rewards cannot distinguish better attempts. With mechanism-level skills, 46.5% of sampled groups contain both successful and failed attempts, compared with 39.0% with near-answer hints. The latter produce more groups in which every attempt succeeds (Appendix 9.1 ). Their higher success rate therefore also comes with more groups that provide no reward difference for learning. Providing concrete answers also changes what the policy needs to do during training. These answers allow it to skip many steps required for independent repair, including locating the relevant code and deciding how to modify it. Providing concrete answers reduces the average number of tokens per rollout by 40.8% relative to GRPO, compared with 14.5% for mechanism-level skills. The trajectories are much shorter. However, they can leave out too many steps needed to solve the task independently. At evaluation, the policy must complete these steps without assistance. The model trained with concrete answers performs worse than GRPO after skills are removed (Appendix 9.2 ).

sections.heading: Early evolution targets context management and patch submission.
sections.text: Reading and search tools limit the text returned in each call, preserving context for later repair steps. Editing tools apply changes directly, reducing the need for shell commands that can fail because of quoting or syntax errors. The first proposal containing these tools raises the pass rate by 13.7% and the trainable rate by 7.4%. Later proposals add tools that generate patches and display code changes, helping the policy prepare and check its submission. Hooks flag repeated actions and remind the policy to reserve steps for checking and submission. The accepted changes form H 1 H_{1} (Table 12 ).

sections.heading: Later evolution focuses on testing and revising repairs.
sections.text: With H 1 H_{1} kept fixed, the policy runs fewer verification tests in the second epoch despite having a testing tool and reminders (Appendix 9.3 ). The teacher adds automatic testing to the tool that prepares the patch. It selects and runs tests related to the changed code. A hook reports failures and reminds the policy to inspect them before submission. This proposal raises the pass rate by 6.3% and the trainable rate by 7.4%. Revised budget reminders discourage repeatedly running every test in the repository while still encouraging tests for the current repair. Another proposal helps the policy undo unsuccessful edits. When a Git command for undoing changes is blocked, a hook recommends the new restore_file tool. This tool restores one file to its original version while preserving edits to other files, so the policy does not have to discard its other work. Both proposals improve the two rates and become part of H 2 H_{2} (Table 14 ).

sections.heading: A rejected proposal.
sections.text: One proposal adds a hook that asks the policy to compare its patch with the task requirements and identify parts that have not been checked. It raises the pass rate by 2.7% but lowers the trainable rate by 7.0%, so it is rejected. In a later round, the teacher combines review with view_diff . This tool displays the lines added, changed, or deleted in selected files, letting the policy inspect its actual edits during review. The later proposal improves both rates and is accepted. A component from a rejected proposal can therefore be reconsidered in a later proposal. Appendix 9.8 gives the remaining rejected proposals and the complete evolution record.

sections.heading: Adding H 2 H_{2} at evaluation improves performance.
sections.text: Skill-Mechanism benefits from H 2 H_{2} on all three benchmarks, although it was trained only with H 0 H_{0} . Its Verified score rises from 52.2% to 54.2%. This improvement comes from changing the tools and hooks, without any additional policy training.

sections.heading: Training with the harness brings larger gains.
sections.text: Switching from H 0 H_{0} to H 2 H_{2} at evaluation raises HarnessAdapt-RL’s Verified score by 4.8 percentage points, compared with 2.0 percentage points for Skill-Mechanism. The same pattern holds on Multilingual and Pro. The difference between these gains is statistically significant when the three benchmarks are combined (Appendix 9.4 ). These results support training the policy with the tools and hooks it will use at deployment.

sections.heading: Removing the evolved tools and hooks lowers performance.
sections.text: Replacing H 2 H_{2} with H 0 H_{0} reduces HarnessAdapt-RL’s pass@1 by 4.8, 7.7, and 4.7 percentage points on Verified, Multilingual, and Pro, respectively. These drops occur without any change to the policy weights. Retaining the evolved tools and hooks is therefore necessary to preserve the trained agent’s full performance. The deployed model–harness pair consists of the trained policy and these tools and hooks, with skills removed.

sections.heading: 4.6 Can the Evolved Harness Be Reused for Training?
sections.text: {wrapfloat} figureR0.48 Figure 4 : Pass@1 differences (percentage points) from HarnessAdapt-RL. Frozen- H 2 H_{2} +Mechanism and Pre-Evolved both train with fixed harnesses and mechanism-level skills, then remove skills at evaluation. We compare reusing H 2 H_{2} with searching for a harness before policy training. Frozen- H 2 H_{2} +Mechanism reuses H 2 H_{2} discovered by HarnessAdapt-RL. Pre-Evolved instead searches with the base policy fixed, using the same search steps and tasks as HarnessAdapt-RL. After obtaining their harnesses, both variants train a new policy from the same base model. Their tools and hooks remain fixed throughout training. We provide mechanism-level skills on the same schedule as in the full method (Section 4.1 ). Frozen- H 2 H_{2} +Mechanism reaches 56.8%, 38.3%, and 38.9% on Verified, Multilingual, and Pro, respectively. These scores are within 1.0 percentage point of HarnessAdapt-RL on every benchmark (Figure 4 ). They also exceed Pre-Evolved by 1.6, 5.3, and 1.9 percentage points. Thus, reusing the harness discovered during policy training gives better results than using the harness found before training. Frozen- H 2 H_{2} +Mechanism achieves similar scores to HarnessAdapt-RL. However, it reuses a harness that HarnessAdapt-RL has already discovered during policy training. In our experiments, searching with the fixed base policy does not produce a harness with the same performance. The strong reuse result therefore depends on first discovering H 2 H_{2} through evolution during training. Once H 2 H_{2} is available, this evolution does not need to be repeated in the new training run.

sections.heading: Skills and policy learning.
sections.text: Voyager builds reusable skills from interaction [ Wang et al., 2024 ] , while SkillRL combines skill evolution with reinforcement learning [ Xia et al., 2026 ] . Agentic Context Engineering (ACE) maintains a playbook of strategies and updates it using feedback from the agent’s interactions [ Zhang et al., 2026 ] . Socratic-SWE uses skills derived from trajectories to generate training tasks [ Xiao et al., 2026 ] . Hindsight Hint Distillation trains on trajectories generated with hints, while PATS adjusts guidance to the current policy [ Wang et al., 2026 , Shi et al., 2026 ] . Both remove this guidance at deployment. We compare near-answer hints, mechanism-level skills, and general skills from a skill bank in software repair. Our comparison focuses on the trained model’s performance after skills are removed.

sections.heading: Harness design and optimization.
sections.text: Tool interfaces and feedback affect agent behavior [ Yang et al., 2024 , Shinn et al., 2023 , Madaan et al., 2023 ] . Meta-Harness automates harness search using earlier candidates and their execution trajectories [ Lee et al., 2026a ] . Retrospective Harness Optimization (RHO) updates skills and tools from past trajectories, selecting changes through the agent’s own preferences without external grading [ Pan et al., 2026 ] . Other methods use revision history, reference trajectories, or interactions across tasks to guide changes [ Lee et al., 2026b , Jiang et al., 2026 , Du et al., 2026 ] . These methods keep model weights fixed during harness optimization. We evolve tools and hooks during policy training. The teacher uses trajectories from the updated policy to propose changes for newly observed problems. Our experiments compare this approach with search under a fixed base policy.

sections.heading: Policy training and harness adaptation.
sections.text: CoEvolve adapts training data alongside the policy [ Yang et al., 2026 ] , while SEARL jointly optimizes the policy and tool graph memory [ Feng et al., 2026 ] . ClawGym II studies reinforcement learning with complex harnesses [ Song et al., 2026 ] . Co-Harness alternates harness updates with supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on trajectories generated by the improved harness [ Chen et al., 2026 ] . HarnessAdapt-RL combines GRPO with tool and hook selection based on the pass rate and trainable rate. A proposal is accepted only if at least one observed rate improves and neither decreases. We also examine which components are needed at deployment. We test whether skill gains persist after removal and how removing the evolved tools and hooks affects performance.

sections.heading: 6 Conclusion
sections.text: We introduced HarnessAdapt-RL, which trains coding agents with GRPO and adapts their harnesses from training trajectories. It generates task-specific skills and evolves tools and hooks as the policy learns. A proposal is accepted only if it improves the observed pass rate or the observed trainable rate without lowering either. With a 9B base model, HarnessAdapt-RL improves pass@1 over GRPO by 9.8, 12.6, and 6.4 percentage points on SWE-bench Verified, Multilingual, and Pro. It also outperforms OpenHands-GRPO. Mechanism-level skills outperform near-answer hints and general skills from a skill bank after skills are removed. Evolving tools and hooks during policy training performs better than searching only before training or keeping the first-epoch harness fixed. Once discovered, the evolved harness can support a new training run without further evolution. Removing its tools and hooks at deployment lowers pass@1 by up to 7.7 percentage points. Training therefore produces a model–harness pair: the trained policy and the evolved tools and hooks, with task-specific skills removed at deployment.

sections.heading: Data Availability
sections.text: The model weights, evolved harness, training code, and data are available at https://github.com/lingxiaotang/HarnessAdapt-RL .

sections.heading: Limitations
sections.text: All tasks are software repair from SWE-bench-style benchmarks, and the skills, tools, and hooks were derived for this setting. We have not tested whether the same procedure produces useful support in other agent domains, such as web navigation or data analysis. We also use a single 9B base model. We do not know whether larger models, which may already handle many of the operations that our tools package, would benefit from harness evolution to the same extent, or whether the preferred form of guidance would stay the same across model families. Each configuration is trained once. The three repetitions are evaluations of a fixed trained checkpoint, not independent training runs (Appendix 8.4 ). The reported confidence intervals characterize task-level variation for these checkpoints; they do not quantify variability across training seeds or independent harness-search runs. Candidate selection uses observed pass and trainable rates from a finite rollout comparison (Appendix 8.2 ). Its acceptance rule is not a significance test: an observed improvement need not imply an improvement in the underlying success or trainability probabilities. Rollout noise and repeated candidate search can therefore affect which changes are retained. The statistical analysis of the final evaluations does not remove this uncertainty from the search process.

The 512-task assisted subset is drawn uniformly at random from the pool, without reference to task difficulty, and is held fixed across configurations. sections.heading: Teacher inputs.
sections.text: Each assisted task visit starts a skill-generation request, which returns a Markdown response. The teacher sees the issue and trajectory records, including any source code and test output shown in those records. It has no direct repository access and cannot inspect hidden tests or grader artifacts (Table 4 ). Only the resulting skill is shown to the policy, and neither the teacher nor any training skill is used at evaluation. For mechanism-level skills, the skill describes the repair mechanism rather than reproducing the diff.

sections.heading: Trajectory pairing.
sections.text: The teacher compares two of the four preparation rollouts of a task, preferably one success and one failure. When all rollouts succeed, the pair consists of two successes and the skill describes the shared successful mechanism. When all rollouts fail, the pair consists of two failures, and the teacher decides from the issue and the partial progress in the trajectories which repair direction the skill describes. The skill format is the same in all three cases.

sections.heading: Guidance variants.
sections.text: The three variants differ in both specificity and evidence scope. Near-answer hints name the file, function, and variables involved and state the concrete edit. Each mechanism-level skill describes a single repair mechanism, with repository names, paths, symbols, literal code, and diff text removed. Both are generated from a single task, using its issue and the two trajectories with the test outputs they contain. Skill-bank guidance instead summarizes general procedures that recur across tasks. The teacher reads the task reports from the current batch together with the previous meta-skill bank and rewrites the bank into at most ten procedures within 1,000 English words. Evidence identifiers are removed before the bank is shown to the policy. Section 4.3 compares the training and evaluation results of these variants. For Skill-Mechanism, only the Task-specific Skill section of the teacher’s response is injected. Appendix 10.1 gives the full prompts for all three variants.

sections.heading: Representative outputs.
sections.text: Appendix 10.2 shows representative teacher outputs for each guidance type.

sections.heading: Length and leakage control.
sections.text: Excluding the three field labels, mechanism-level skills average 100.67 whitespace-delimited words, with a median of 100 and a maximum of 154. We screen mechanism-level skills for answer-locating paths, symbols, and code. Near-answer hints intentionally include such details and are not subject to this restriction. A mechanism-level skill that fails the screen is regenerated up to three times. If it still fails, the task is trained without a skill.

sections.heading: Second epoch and Skill-Gated.
sections.text: Skills for the second epoch are regenerated rather than reused from the first. Skill-Gated invokes the teacher only when all four preparation attempts of a task fail, and generates the skill from two of these failed trajectories chosen at random.

sections.heading: 7.3 Execution Limits and Submission
sections.text: All configurations share the same execution budgets. Training rollouts allow a 64K context (65,536 tokens) and at most 60 turns, while evaluation allows a 128K context (131,072 tokens) and at most 150 turns. Both use temperature 1.0. The shorter training budget bounds the cost of collecting multiple rollouts per task for each GRPO update. Evaluation makes a single attempt per held-out task, so the longer budget leaves the trained policy room to read, verify, and submit. Prior SWE agents also use shorter context or turn budgets during training than at evaluation [ Yang et al., 2025b , Cao et al., 2025 ] . Shorter interaction horizons can also improve reinforcement-learning stability [ Kim et al., 2026 ] .

sections.heading: Truncation and submission.
sections.text: A trajectory is truncated if it exceeds either the turn limit or the context limit, and is counted once if it exceeds both. A submission made on the final allowed turn counts as complete. The prepare_patch tool writes the selected source changes to patch.txt but neither submits nor scores the repair. Submission is a separate Bash action: ⬇ echo COMPLETE_TASK_AND_SUBMIT_FINAL_OUTPUT && cat patch . txt The submitted patch is then applied and tested in a fresh task container.

sections.heading: 8.1 Hyperparameters and Schedule
sections.text: Policy training uses GRPO implemented in slime [ Zhu et al., 2025 ] , with a constant learning rate of 10 − 6 10^{-6} . GLM-5.3-Flash [ Z.ai, 2026 ] generates skills through OpenCode [ OpenCode Contributors, 2026 ] , and GPT-5.6 Sol [ OpenAI, 2026 ] designs and implements tool and hook proposals through Codex [ OpenAI, 2025 ] . The release configuration records the provider model identifiers glm-5.3-flash and gpt-5.6-sol . The setup guide describes the provider endpoints and credentials used by the two CLIs; inference with the released model– H 2 H_{2} pair requires neither teacher. These identifiers do not pin immutable teacher snapshots, and the historical CLI package versions were not preserved. The reproduction setup therefore requires explicit CLI versions to be supplied and records the installed versions. Training runs for two epochs over the 1,058-task pool. Each epoch consists of 23 updates of 46 tasks ( 23 × 46 = 1,058 23\times 46=1{,}058 ), so every batch is full and no task is repeated or padded within an epoch. Updates 1–23 form the first epoch and updates 24–46 the second, for 2,116 task visits in total. The first epoch assists all tasks, and the second assists the fixed 512-task subset with regenerated skills. GRPO samples 8 rollouts per task, and every other trained configuration samples 4. sections.heading: 8.2 Candidate Generation
sections.text: In each evolution round, the teacher receives all preparation trajectories from that round, the current harness, and the outcomes of earlier proposals, without subsampling. Within a single call, it analyzes the trajectory evidence, selects a supported problem, and designs and implements one candidate to address it. It returns the diagnosis, design rationale, and concrete code or edits, or no_change when the evidence or available interfaces do not support a useful modification. A bundle may contain several tools and hooks, with corresponding usage instructions, when they serve the same repair workflow. Appendix 10.3 gives the full proposal prompt. The generated code is used without human modification. Before any rollout comparison, we check the candidate’s output format, tool schemas, module loading, and a software smoke test. Tools and hooks outside the proposal must remain byte-identical to the current harness, and task-specific skill text must be unchanged. A candidate that fails any check is discarded without comparison. The comparison follows Section 3.3 . Both harnesses are run on fresh rollouts under the same policy, tasks, skills, and rollout budget. The trainable rate is the share of sampled rollouts eligible for policy updates, and the pass rate is the share whose patch passes the task tests. We exclude truncated rollouts from the trainable-rate count, motivated by the loss masking of overlong trajectories in prior LLM and agent RL work [ Yu et al., 2025 , Luo et al., 2025 , Cao et al., 2025 ] . For this metric, we additionally require the remaining rollouts in each task group to include both successful and failed attempts. When this condition holds, the remaining rollouts are eligible, subject to the unknown-reward exclusion in Appendix 8.3 . If the remaining attempts all succeed or all fail, none are trainable. The denominator for the trainable rate includes all sampled rollouts, including those excluded by these rules. Successful rollouts in an all-success group count toward the pass rate but not the trainable rate. Rollouts with unknown rewards count as non-passing and remain in the denominator. A candidate is accepted if neither observed rate decreases and at least one strictly increases. If both remain unchanged, it is rejected. Each accepted bundle updates the retained harness. The first-epoch harness H 1 H_{1} contains seven tools and four hooks (Table 12 ). The second-epoch harness H 2 H_{2} , used by HarnessAdapt-RL at update 45, contains eight tools and five hooks (Table 14 ). Each training epoch begins with at most five harness-evolution rounds. A rejected candidate or a no_change response also uses one round. The retained harness is fixed for the remaining policy training in that epoch.

HarnessAdapt-RL additionally collects comparison rollouts in rounds that propose a candidate. Each comparison uses 184 fresh rollouts per harness on the same 46 tasks, with four rollouts per task. Comparison rollouts are discarded once the decision is made. Rounds that return no_change require no comparison. Failed requests are not replaced: an update keeps its scheduled rollouts and does not resample to fill a group. A rollout with an unknown reward is neither a pass nor a confirmed failure. We exclude its group from the policy update instead of assigning a reward of 0. Teacher retries that repair a skill’s format do not add training rollouts. In the skill-training run, training rollouts record 14 summary errors, 11 unknown rewards, and 3 timeouts, and first-epoch preparation rollouts record 6 summary errors and 6 unknown rewards. Because these events overlap, we do not sum them into a single failure count.

sections.heading: 8.4 Training Runs and Evaluation
sections.text: Each configuration is trained once. We evaluate the checkpoint from update 45, the last saved checkpoint before training ends at update 46. Checkpoints are saved every five updates, and this choice was made before evaluation. Each evaluation is repeated three times, with one attempt per task in each run. We report the mean pass@1, keeping failed or unfinished attempts in the denominator as incorrect. Appendix 9.4 describes the confidence intervals. Learning curves evaluate Verified every five updates under the same protocol. Their final points equal the reported scores in Tables 1 and 11 . Avg. is the unweighted mean of the three reported benchmark scores. The training statistics in Appendices 9.1 and 9.2 cover all 46 updates of the same runs. They describe sampled groups and rollouts, not unique tasks or independent training replicates.

Dashed lines mark the boundary between the two training epochs. Figure 2 in Section 4.3 compares the three forms of guidance. Figure 7 compares guidance coverage. Skill-Gated provides a skill only when all attempts collected before skill generation fail. Skill-Mechanism also provides skills to tasks with successful attempts. Skill-Mechanism and Skill-Gated share the mechanism-level skill prompt, base harness, training schedule, and evaluation protocol. They differ in guidance coverage and in the trajectories used to generate guidance. Skill-Gated ends at 47.2% on Verified, close to GRPO’s 47.8% and below Skill-Mechanism’s 52.2%. sections.heading: Comparison protocol and reporting.
sections.text: Each epoch allows at most five harness-evolution rounds, starting from H 0 H_{0} in epoch 1 and H 1 H_{1} in epoch 2. In each comparison, the candidate and current harness use the same policy checkpoint, 46-task batch, skills, and rollout budget. Each side generates four rollouts per task, for 184 rollouts. The two rates use all sampled rollouts as the denominator, with trainability defined in Appendix 8.2 . After selection, fresh training rollouts are collected under the retained harness for the policy update. Comparison rollouts are not reused for training. Figure 3 and Table 15 report relative percentage changes. Numerical summaries are rounded to one decimal place. sections.heading: First-epoch progression.
sections.text: Rounds 1, 2, and 5 are accepted. Round 1 adds reading, search, editing, file creation, and checking tools. Round 2 adds patch preparation and hooks for budget use, repeated actions, and validation. Batched inspection in round 3 lowers the pass rate, while the review proposal in round 4 lowers the trainable rate, so both are rejected. Round 5 accepts review together with diff inspection. The accepted candidates raise the pass rate by 5.6%–13.7% and the trainable rate by 7.4%–7.8% relative to the current harness in each round. The resulting H 1 H_{1} has seven tools and four hooks (Table 12 ) and is retained for the rest of the epoch. Frozen- H 1 H_{1} and H 1 H_{1} +Mechanism also use this harness.

Their relative gains are 3.5%–6.3% in pass rate and 3.2%–7.4% in trainable rate. Round 4 requests an additional policy-run test when automatic selection provides no verification evidence. It is rejected because the pass rate falls by 2.3% despite a 1.6% trainable-rate gain. Round 5 produces no candidate. The retained H 2 H_{2} has eight tools and five hooks and is used for subsequent training and evaluation. Its six original tools other than prepare_patch , and its progress_guard hook, are unchanged. sections.heading: Rejected proposals.
sections.text: The batched-reading tool inspect_windows combines two to four source windows in one call. The policy supplies each file, line offset, and window length, so the tool does not locate relevant code automatically. The accompanying inspection_checkpoint hook asks the policy to summarize its current hypothesis and an unresolved observation after five consecutive successful reading or search steps. Other actions reset this sequence. The tool therefore combines planned reads without choosing where the policy should look next. The first-epoch review proposal asks the policy to compare the repair against task requirements and identify gaps in its checks. That candidate fails the acceptance rule, while a later candidate combining review with diff inspection is accepted. In the second epoch, the rejected patch-preparation rule explicitly requests another policy-run test when automatic test selection supplies no verification evidence. The retained delivery_evidence hook instead bases its suggestions on the observed checks and remaining budget. Further policy-run checks remain available through run_check . Table 15 gives all proposal outcomes.

sections.heading: First-epoch tool limits.
sections.text: read_file returns 60 lines by default and at most 200. grep returns up to 60 matching lines by default and at most 100. view_diff shows 120 lines per page by default and at most 200. Reading and diff outputs also have character limits. run_check allows at most 45 seconds, preserves pipeline failures, and reports runner problems, zero-test signals, and timeouts. A zero exit code alone does not establish that the task requirements were tested. In H 1 H_{1} , prepare_patch checks patch structure without running behavioral tests. Further edits require patch regeneration.

sections.heading: First-epoch hook triggers.
sections.text: The three budget tiers begin at 30, 12, and 5 remaining turns, or 24,576, 12,288, and 6,144 remaining context tokens, respectively. Reminders occur only on entry to a tighter tier, while turns remain. progress_guard requires identical calls and results in three different turns within a 12-turn window. It gives at most two reminders, once per signature. validation_feedback allows two check-failure reminders, one preparation-failure reminder, and one validation summary after successful preparation. semantic_review runs once. Shell-check recognition is heuristic, so missing records do not prove that no check occurred.

sections.heading: Tests during patch preparation.
sections.text: In H 2 H_{2} , prepare_patch keeps the same file-selection interface. After preparing the patch, it ranks tracked Python test files using the changed paths and diff, excluding setup files, runners, and edited files. Matching filenames add three points and matching parent directories add one point per changed file. A textual reference to an extracted function or class name adds two points per candidate test file. Names come from diff hunk headers and added or removed definitions. The tool retains up to eight distinct names longer than three characters, excluding names beginning with two underscores. It keeps the top five tests scoring at least two, breaking ties by shorter paths and then alphabetical order. It runs up to two selected test files or modules within 25 seconds, using tests/runtests.py , pytest, or bin/test , depending on the repository. Returned evidence includes the command, status, exit code, failure summary, elapsed time, and log location. Results are cached by patch content, working directory, and command, with reuse explicitly marked. Selection provides partial verification evidence, not guaranteed coverage or the official task score. The policy can run additional checks through run_check . Patch preparation and tests have separate statuses. Preparation can return ok: true while tests fail, time out, or cannot run. The policy reads related_test_run for the test outcome. The tool also reports line changes and flags files with at least 100 deletions and at least twice as many deletions as additions. This prompts inspection without declaring the change incorrect.

sections.heading: Validation feedback.
sections.text: delivery_evidence replaces semantic_review . It tracks editing, file creation, restoration, and shell source changes recognized from command patterns. A tracked non-temporary source edit resets the check list. Records distinguish tests, assertion-based scripts, and print-only scripts. After successful preparation, the hook summarizes these records, related test results, large deletions, and remaining budget. It suggests inspecting failures, adding a focused check, or submitting, according to the evidence and budget. At most three summaries are emitted, with a newly tracked edit required after the first. The summary covers observed events, not every possible edit or check. validation_feedback retains failure feedback but delegates the preparation summary to this hook.

sections.heading: File recovery.
sections.text: restore_file restores one tracked regular file from the Git index, which the task rules prohibit the policy from changing. It discards that file’s edits and can recreate a deleted file. Other files, the index, and patch.txt remain unchanged, so recovery requires patch regeneration. Untracked files, directories, symbolic links, and conflicted entries are rejected. After a blocked Git recovery or comparison command, recovery_hint suggests restoration, diff inspection, or preserving edits before restoration, as appropriate. It emits at most two reminders.

sections.heading: Accompanying harness instructions.
sections.text: H 2 H_{2} explains automatic tests, failure handling, file recovery, and the limits of print-only checks. It directs existing-file edits through edit_file and preserves focused testing while discouraging repeated full-suite runs. These general harness instructions remain at evaluation, unlike temporary task-specific skills. The system prompt is unchanged.

sections.heading: Runtime and submission.
sections.text: Hooks add feedback without teacher calls, repair commands, or submission blocking. Automatic tests run inside prepare_patch . Submission remains a separate native Bash action (Appendix 7.3 ).

sections.heading: 10 Prompts and Teacher Outputs
sections.text: This appendix documents the teacher prompts and representative outputs. Placeholders in double braces are filled in at run time. Prompts are reproduced as full-width figures, with long instructions split between complete paragraphs or list items. All prompt text is preserved.

sections.heading: 10.1 Skill Generation Prompts
sections.text: The prompts below correspond to the guidance variants in Appendix 7.2 . Near-answer hints and mechanism-level skills use evidence from a single task. The skill bank combines evidence across tasks. Figures 9 – 15 reproduce the instructions and input templates.

sections.text: Figure 16 shows one representative output for each guidance type. Near-answer hints specify code changes. Mechanism-level skills explain the repair mechanism without code identifiers. Use these definitions : - Pass rate : the number of sampled rollouts that pass the task evaluator , divided by the total number of sampled rollouts . - Trainable rollout ratio : the number of sampled rollouts retained by the actual training postprocessing with a nonzero policy - loss token mask , divided by the total number of sampled rollouts . Use the recorded evaluator outcomes and actual postprocessing rules and masks ; when these are unavailable , state the uncertainty . If the training pipeline excludes groups with identical rewards , both all - success and all - failure groups may be excluded from policy loss . Report Issue Back to Abstract Download PDF Contents Reading mode Colour theme License: CC BY 4.0 arXiv:2610.28069v1 [cs.SE] 20 Oct 2026 1]Zhejiang University 2]LIGHTSPEED 3]Independent Researcher \headercontent Code: github.com/lingxiaotang/HarnessAdapt-RL Training the Whole Agent, Not Just the Model Lingxiao Tang Wei Tao Yiwen Guo Lingfeng Bao Affiliation: [ Affiliation: [ Affiliation: [ October 2026 Abstract Training coding agents typically updates the policy while keeping the harness fixed. During training, trajectories reveal flawed repair strategies and interaction problems that vary across tasks and change as the policy learns. We introduce HarnessAdapt-RL, which trains the policy and adapts its harness during reinforcement learning. For flawed repair strategies, a frozen teacher generates task-specific mechanism-level skills. For interaction problems recurring across tasks, a separate teacher model evolves tools and hooks, keeping each change only if it improves the observed pass rate or the observed trainable rate without lowering either. The policy trains with the adapted harness, and its new trajectories guide further adaptation. With a 9B base model, HarnessAdapt-RL improves pass@1 over GRPO by 9.8, 12.6, and 6.4 percentage points on SWE-bench Verified, Multilingual, and Pro, and outperforms GRPO with the human-designed OpenHands harness. Gains from mechanism-level skills persist after their removal at evaluation. Re-evolving tools and hooks as the policy changes outperforms freezing early versions. Removing them at deployment, in contrast, costs up to 7.7 percentage points. Training therefore produces a model–harness pair: the trained policy and the evolved tools and hooks, with skills removed at deployment. 1 1 footnotetext: Work is done during internship at LIGHTSPEED. 2 2 footnotetext: Equal contribution: Lingxiao Tang and Wei Tao. 3 3 footnotetext: Corresponding authors: Yiwen Guo ( guoyiwen89@gmail.com ) and Lingfeng Bao ( lingfengbao@zju.edu.cn ). 1 Introduction A coding agent operates as a model–harness pair: the model selects actions, while the harness provides guidance, tools, and runtime feedback. Agent training typically improves the policy while keeping the harness fixed [ Jain et al., 2025 , Yang et al., 2025a , Xi et al., 2026 ] . The harness shapes the interaction trajectories used to update the policy, affecting both the effectiveness of training and the performance of the trained agent [ Chen et al., 2026 ] . Prior work has explored both harness optimization and training-time guidance. Previous methods optimize the harness while keeping the policy fixed [ Lee et al., 2026a , Jiang et al., 2026 , Du et al., 2026 ] . Other methods use skills and training guidance to improve policy learning from trajectories [ Xiao et al., 2026 , Wang et al., 2026 , Shi et al., 2026 ] . Co-Harness alternates harness updates with supervised fine-tuning on trajectories generated by the improved harness [ Chen et al., 2026 ] . We study harness adaptation during reinforcement learning for coding agents. During training, trajectories expose flawed repair strategies, such as incorrect diagnoses or fixes that only address symptoms. They also reveal interaction problems, such as failed editing commands, excessive output, or insufficient verification. This evidence can guide changes to skills, tools, and runtime hooks that help alleviate these problems. As the problems vary across tasks and change with the policy, the harness needs to adapt throughout training (Appendix 9.3 ). We therefore ask how to design skills for policy learning, how to design and select tools and hooks as the policy changes, and which harness components to retain at deployment. To address these questions, we introduce HarnessAdapt-RL , which trains the policy and adapts its harness during reinforcement learning. In our setting, skills are textual guidance supplied to the policy during training. First, we compare three skill-guidance variants and use mechanism-level skills that explain when and why a repair strategy applies without providing concrete answers. A frozen teacher model generates these task-specific skills from training trajectories. Second, a separate teacher model identifies recurring interaction and feedback problems across tasks and proposes changes to tools and hooks. Harness selection considers both task success and the availability of rollouts for policy updates (Section 3.3 ). Each proposal is kept only if it improves the observed pass rate or the observed trainable rate without lowering either (Appendix 8.2 ). We refer to this process as tool and hook evolution. The policy then trains with GRPO [ Shao et al., 2024 ] on fresh rollouts using the evolved tools and hooks and skills for assisted tasks. Trajectories from the updated policy guide later proposals. Third, we examine which components should remain at deployment. We evaluate the policy after removing skills and compare performance with and without the evolved tools and hooks. With a 9B base model, HarnessAdapt-RL improves pass@1 over GRPO by 9.8, 12.6, and 6.4 percentage points on SWE-bench Verified [ Chowdhury et al., 2024 ] , Multilingual [ Yang et al., 2025a ] , and Pro [ Deng et al., 2025 ] . It also outperforms GRPO training with the human-designed OpenHands harness on all three benchmarks. Under the same base harness, models trained with mechanism-level skills perform best among the three skill-guidance variants when evaluated without skills. Re-evolving tools and hooks as the policy changes outperforms keeping their early versions fixed. Holding the trained policy weights fixed, removing the evolved tools and hooks at evaluation reduces pass@1 by up to 7.7 percentage points. Together, these results show that gains from skills persist after their removal, while the evolved tools and hooks remain necessary for full performance at deployment. Our contributions are threefold: • Skill design for policy learning. We compare three skill-guidance variants and find that mechanism-level skills yield the best repair performance after guidance is removed. • Tool and hook evolution during reinforcement learning. We use current-policy trajectories to propose tools and hooks and select changes using both the pass rate and the trainable rate. • Training and deploying the model–harness pair. We show that gains from skill guidance persist after its removal, while retaining the evolved tools and hooks at deployment preserves the complete performance. 2 Problem Formulation Agent and harness. An agent combines a policy with a harness that provides skill guidance, tools, and runtime feedback. A teacher model uses current-policy trajectories to generate task-specific skills for flawed repair strategies. A separate teacher model proposes changes to tools and hooks for recurring interaction problems across tasks. We accept a proposal only if it improves the observed pass rate or the observed trainable rate without lowering either. The policy then trains through GRPO [ Shao et al., 2024 ] on rollouts generated with the adapted harness. Its new trajectories then guide subsequent harness adaptation. 3.1 Policy-Adaptive Repair Skills We generate skills from training trajectories to guide the policy’s repair strategies. Prior work finds that many skills do not improve software engineering performance [ Han et al., 2026 ] . We therefore compare three ways of generating skills and assess the model’s performance after training, with the skills removed. We first evaluate a skill bank with a fixed capacity, based on prior work that extracts reusable strategies from trajectories [ Suzgun et al., 2025 , Xia et al., 2026 ] . The teacher reviews trajectories across training tasks and adds, removes, merges, or updates general repair skills. This approach does not consistently improve performance over GRPO, suggesting that these skills are too general to help with individual repair tasks (Section 4.3 ). A more task-specific alternative is to provide near-answer hints with concrete code changes, including variable, function, or class names. These hints produce shorter trajectories and higher training success, but the trained model performs worse than GRPO when evaluated without them (Section 4.3 , Appendix 9.2 ). We therefore propose mechanism-level skills that focus on the policy’s flawed repair strategies while leaving the policy to work out the concrete solution. For each assisted task, the teacher model compares two trajectories from the current policy. Using the issue and the evidence in these trajectories, it identifies a repair strategy and explains when and why it applies. The resulting mechanism-level skill retains the technical reasoning behind the repair but omits repository paths, code symbols, and literal code. This guides the policy’s repair strategy while leaving code localization and implementation to the policy. Appendices 7.2 and 10.2 provide generation details and examples. 3.2 Evolving Tools and Hooks for Policy Training Training trajectories also reveal recurring problems in how the policy interacts with its environment. The teacher uses this evidence to propose changes to tools and hooks. To support both task performance and policy learning, it uses the pass rate and the trainable rate to guide these proposals. Trainable rollouts are those usable for policy updates (Appendix 8.2 ). The teacher uses current-policy trajectories and the current harness to develop a proposal in four steps. (1) Find recurring problems. The teacher compares trajectories across tasks to identify recurring problems in tool use and feedback. (2) Inspect trajectories. The teacher reads the tool calls, outputs, and hook messages to understand each recurring problem. For example, the policy runs fewer verification tests later in training, even though it has testing tools and receives reminders. The teacher inspects these trajectories to understand why the policy skips tests before submitting a patch. (3) Design changes. To address the identified problems, the teacher can propose one or more tools, hooks, or a combination of both. Tools package repair operations into reusable actions. Hooks give the policy feedback during execution. In the testing example, the teacher modifies the patch-preparation tool so that it automatically runs related tests when preparing a patch. A hook then reports any test failures and reminds the policy to check them before submission. (4) Implement the proposal. The teacher implements the proposed changes as a candidate harness for evaluation. As the policy learns, its new trajectories guide further adaptation of tools and hooks (Appendix 9.3 ). Appendix 8.2 provides the full proposal procedure. 3.3 Training-Aware Harness Selection We select harness changes to support both task success and policy learning. GRPO uses reward differences among attempts on the same task to update the policy [ Shao et al., 2024 , Yu et al., 2025 ] . Groups in which all attempts succeed or all fail provide no reward contrast for policy updates. Successful rollouts in an all-success group therefore count toward the pass rate without contributing to policy learning. To account for training usability, we also measure the trainable rate, the fraction of sampled rollouts eligible for policy updates (Appendix 8.2 ). We evaluate each proposal by running the candidate and current harnesses with the same policy, tasks, skills, and rollout budget. We accept the proposal only if it improves the observed pass rate or the observed trainable rate without lowering either. These rates are empirical fractions from the finite comparison rollouts; the acceptance rule does not test statistical significance. Accepted changes are used for subsequent policy training. Otherwise, training continues with the current tools and hooks. Changes from a rejected proposal can be proposed again in later rounds. Policy updates. After selection, we collect fresh rollouts with the selected tools and hooks, providing skills for assisted tasks. Preparation and comparison rollouts are not reused for training. We update the policy with GRPO using the new rollouts, with loss computed only on policy-generated tokens [ Shao et al., 2024 ] . Evolution across training epochs. Each training epoch begins with up to five rounds of tool and hook evolution. After each round, we update the policy using the selected tools and hooks. These tools and hooks then stay fixed for the remaining training steps in that epoch. The first epoch produces H 1 H_{1} . The second epoch starts from H 1 H_{1} and uses trajectories from the updated policy to evolve H 2 H_{2} . 4 Experiments 4.1 Experimental Setup Training setup. Voyager builds reusable skills from interaction [ Wang et al., 2024 ] , while SkillRL combines skill evolution with reinforcement learning [ Xia et al., 2026 ] . Agentic Context Engineering (ACE) maintains a playbook of strategies and updates it using feedback from the agent’s interactions [ Zhang et al., 2026 ] . Socratic-SWE uses skills derived from trajectories to generate training tasks [ Xiao et al., 2026 ] . Hindsight Hint Distillation trains on trajectories generated with hints, while PATS adjusts guidance to the current policy [ Wang et al., 2026 , Shi et al., 2026 ] . Both remove this guidance at deployment. We compare near-answer hints, mechanism-level skills, and general skills from a skill bank in software repair. Our comparison focuses on the trained model’s performance after skills are removed. Harness design and optimization. Tool interfaces and feedback affect agent behavior [ Yang et al., 2024 , Shinn et al., 2023 , Madaan et al., 2023 ] . Meta-Harness automates harness search using earlier candidates and their execution trajectories [ Lee et al., 2026a ] . Retrospective Harness Optimization (RHO) updates skills and tools from past trajectories, selecting changes through the agent’s own preferences without external grading [ Pan et al., 2026 ] . Other methods use revision history, reference trajectories, or interactions across tasks to guide changes [ Lee et al., 2026b , Jiang et al., 2026 , Du et al., 2026 ] . These methods keep model weights fixed during harness optimization. We evolve tools and hooks during policy training. The teacher uses trajectories from the updated policy to propose changes for newly observed problems. Our experiments compare this approach with search under a fixed base policy. Policy training and harness adaptation. CoEvolve adapts training data alongside the policy [ Yang et al., 2026 ] , while SEARL jointly optimizes the policy and tool graph memory [ Feng et al., 2026 ] . ClawGym II studies reinforcement learning with complex harnesses [ Song et al., 2026 ] . Co-Harness alternates harness updates with supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on trajectories generated by the improved harness [ Chen et al., 2026 ] . HarnessAdapt-RL combines GRPO with tool and hook selection based on the pass rate and trainable rate. A proposal is accepted only if at least one observed rate improves and neither decreases. We also examine which components are needed at deployment. We test whether skill gains persist after removal and how removing the evolved tools and hooks affects performance. 6 Conclusion We introduced HarnessAdapt-RL, which trains coding agents with GRPO and adapts their harnesses from training trajectories. It generates task-specific skills and evolves tools and hooks as the policy learns. A proposal is accepted only if it improves the observed pass rate or the observed trainable rate without lowering either. With a 9B base model, HarnessAdapt-RL improves pass@1 over GRPO by 9.8, 12.6, and 6.4 percentage points on SWE-bench Verified, Multilingual, and Pro. It also outperforms OpenHands-GRPO. Mechanism-level skills outperform near-answer hints and general skills from a skill bank after skills are removed. Evolving tools and hooks during policy training performs better than searching only before training or keeping the first-epoch harness fixed. Once discovered, the evolved harness can support a new training run without further evolution. Removing its tools and hooks at deployment lowers pass@1 by up to 7.7 percentage points. Training therefore produces a model–harness pair: the trained policy and the evolved tools and hooks, with task-specific skills removed at deployment. Data Availability The model weights, evolved harness, training code, and data are available at https://github.com/lingxiaotang/HarnessAdapt-RL . Limitations All tasks are software repair from SWE-bench-style benchmarks, and the skills, tools, and hooks were derived for this setting. We have not tested whether the same procedure produces useful support in other agent domains, such as web navigation or data analysis. We also use a single 9B base model. We do not know whether larger models, which may already handle many of the operations that our tools package, would benefit from harness evolution to the same extent, or whether the preferred form of guidance would stay the same across model families. Each configuration is trained once. The three repetitions are evaluations of a fixed trained checkpoint, not independent training runs (Appendix 8.4 ). The reported confidence intervals characterize task-level variation for these checkpoints; they do not quantify variability across training seeds or independent harness-search runs. Candidate selection uses observed pass and trainable rates from a finite rollout comparison (Appendix 8.2 ). Its acceptance rule is not a significance test: an observed improvement need not imply an improvement in the underlying success or trainability probabilities. Rollout noise and repeated candidate search can therefore affect which changes are retained. The statistical analysis of the final evaluations does not remove this uncertainty from the search process. References Jain et al. Training rollouts allow a 64K context (65,536 tokens) and at most 60 turns, while evaluation allows a 128K context (131,072 tokens) and at most 150 turns. Both use temperature 1.0. The shorter training budget bounds the cost of collecting multiple rollouts per task for each GRPO update. Evaluation makes a single attempt per held-out task, so the longer budget leaves the trained policy room to read, verify, and submit. Prior SWE agents also use shorter context or turn budgets during training than at evaluation [ Yang et al., 2025b , Cao et al., 2025 ] . Shorter interaction horizons can also improve reinforcement-learning stability [ Kim et al., 2026 ] . Truncation and submission. A trajectory is truncated if it exceeds either the turn limit or the context limit, and is counted once if it exceeds both. A submission made on the final allowed turn counts as complete.
